schools.summary: Gill reports three readings of the person addressed and adopts none. Some think, from the connection with the preceding chapter, that the Gentiles are meant, and particularly those among them who seemed to be virtuous and took upon them to be the reprovers of others while doing the same things themselves, as Socrates, Cato and Seneca, who must be inexcusable because they knew better and would be thought to have been so, and so could never be justified before God by their works. Others think the Jews are meant, who despised and condemned the Gentiles and thought themselves to be right. Others think magistrates are designed, whether among Jews or Gentiles, who reprove and punish sin in others and therefore must be supposed to know the law and the nature of sin, so that they are inexcusable and self-condemned when they do the same things, and though they may pass with impunity among men they shall not escape the righteous judgment of God. Calvin takes the reproof to be directed against hypocrites, who dazzle the eyes of men by displays of outward sanctity and even think themselves accepted before God as though they had given him full satisfaction; having stated the grosser vices, Paul now attacks saintlings of this kind, who could not have been included in the first catalogue. The inference, he says, is simple: they knew the judgment of God and yet transgressed the law, so that though one consent not to the vices of others and seem an avowed enemy and reprover of vice, if he is not free from them he can bring forward no defence. He notes the striking resemblance between the two Greek verbs and the enhancing of the sin, since such a man is doubly deserving of condemnation, being guilty of the vices he blames in others; it is a well-known saying that they who scrutinise the life of others lay claim themselves to innocence, temperance and all virtues, and that those are not worthy of any indulgence who allow in themselves what they undertake to correct in others. They condemned themselves, he adds, because in reproving a thief or an adulterer or a slanderer they condemned not merely the persons but the very vices which adhered to themselves. On the opening particle he is candid that most confess it can hardly be accounted for, since the inference from the preceding is not very evident; in his view it is an instance of Hebraism, referring not to what has preceded but to what is to come, not properly an illative but an anticipation of a reason afterwards given, so that the sense is: on this account, inexcusable art thou, O man, whosoever thou be who condemnest another, because in what thou condemnest another thou condemnest thyself.

Henry sets the chapter in its argument: in the former chapter the apostle had represented the state of the Gentile world to be as bad and black as the Jews were ready enough to pronounce it, and now, designing to show that the state of the Jews was very bad too and their sin in many respects more aggravated, he sets himself to show that God would proceed upon equal terms of justice with Jews and Gentiles, and not with such a partial hand as the Jews were apt to think he would use in their favour. He arraigns them first for their censoriousness and self-conceit. Since the apostle expresses himself in general terms, the admonition may reach those many masters, of whatever nation or profession they are, that assume to themselves a power to censure, control and condemn others; but he intends especially the Jews, to whom he applies the general charge later in the chapter, since they were generally a proud sort of people who looked with scorn and contempt upon the poor Gentiles as not worthy to be set with the dogs of their flock, while they were themselves as bad and immoral, and though not idolaters as the Gentiles were, yet sacrilegious. Therefore, he concludes, thou art inexcusable: if the Gentiles, who had but the light of nature, were inexcusable, much more the Jews, who had the light of the law and the revealed will of God, and so had greater helps than the Gentiles.

Clarke's block on this verse is not an exposition of it but an analysis of the chapter's whole course, that the Jew who condemns the Gentiles and considers them utterly unworthy of the blessings of the Gospel is inexcusable because he is guilty of the same crimes and shall not escape the righteous judgment of God; that it is an awful thing to despise the goodness and long-suffering of God which lead to repentance; that God the impartial judge will render to every man according to his works; that Jews and Gentiles will be judged according to their respective advantages and disadvantages; and that in some cases the Gentiles, who had no law, have shown a better disposition than the Jews. Wesley marks the transition, that the apostle now passes from the Gentiles to the Jews until the sixth verse comprises both, and that the Jew is inexcusable seeing knowledge without practice only increases guilt. Having before spoken of the Gentile in the third person, Paul addresses the Jew in the second, but calls him by a common appellation, as not acknowledging him to be a Jew; and to judge here is to censure and condemn, so that in judging the heathen he condemns himself, for he does the same things in effect and in many instances.

Barnes says the design of this and the following chapter is to show that the Jews were no less guilty than the Gentiles and needed the same salvation, since they had greater light and yet did the same things while accusing and condemning the Gentiles as wicked and abandoned and excusing themselves on the ground that they possessed the law and the oracles of God. The force of the opening word has been the subject of much discussion; he takes it to refer not to any particular word or verse in the previous chapter but to the general considerations suggested by a view of the whole case, so that the sense is that since the Jews condemned the Gentiles on the ground that they had the means of knowing their duty, they, being far more favoured, are entirely without excuse for the same things. Inexcusable, he insists, does not mean inexcusable for judging others but without excuse for their own sins before God, under condemnation for their crimes and needing the benefits of another plan of justification. The address O man is general to any man who should do this, but the connection shows that the Jews are especially meant; and the use of the word is an instance of the apostle's skill in argument, since to have named the Jews openly here would have been likely to excite their opposition, so that he approaches the subject gradually, affirms it of man in general, and makes the particular application only when he has advanced so far in the general principles of his argument that it would be impossible for them to evade his conclusions, and then in the most tender and kind as well as convincing manner. The verb rendered judgest is used in the sense of condemning, though it is not a word of equal strength with that rendered condemnest; it implies that they were accustomed to express themselves freely and severely on the character and doom of the Gentiles, whom, as their own writings show, they regarded with abhorrence, considered shut out from the favour of God, and described in terms of the utmost contempt. Ellicott says the description just given of one section of the human race contains implicitly the condemnation of the other, being equally applicable to both, and that by the very act of sitting in judgment upon a fellow-man one passes sentence upon oneself, declaring those acts criminal of which one is oneself guilty; the two Greek words are related to each other much as the summing up of a judge is related to his verdict, in the first sentence being in process of being passed with a possibility of acquittal still, in the second definitely given in a sense adverse to the accused, and another is strictly the other, thy fellow or neighbour. Robertson takes the relative conjunction as because of which thing, notes that the address is literally every one that judgest, in the vocative in apposition with O man, and observes with Lightfoot that Paul begins his discussion of the failure of the Jew to attain the God-kind of righteousness with a general statement applicable to all, as he had done in the discussion of the failure of the Gentiles; the Gentile is readily condemned by the Jew when he sins, and equally so is the Jew condemned by the Gentile in like case. The verb, he adds, does not of itself mean to condemn, but to pick out, separate, approve.

Theodoret argues from the judge's own competence. Although thus situated, he says, if you had received authority from any one to pass sentence, you would punish the transgressors of the law as guilty, so perfect a distinguishment have you between good and its opposite. It becomes you then to be aware that in the very judgment you pronounce on others as sinners you involve yourselves in the same condemnation, for you have not hesitated to fall into the same transgressions.

debates: Who the man addressed is: Gill reports the seemingly virtuous Gentiles such as Socrates, Cato and Seneca, the Jews, and magistrates of either nation without choosing between them, Calvin takes it of hypocrites as a class rather than of a nation, Henry and Barnes hold the general terms to intend the Jews especially, and Robertson and Ellicott keep the statement general and applicable to both sides alike

What the opening Therefore refers to: Barnes says the question has been much discussed and refers it to the general considerations of the whole case rather than to any word or verse, Calvin admits the illative can hardly be accounted for and takes it as a Hebraism pointing forward to a reason given afterwards, and Robertson simply refers it back to the previous chapter

What the verb rendered judgest means: Robertson insists it does not of itself mean to condemn but to pick out, separate or approve, Barnes allows the weaker force but takes it here in the sense of condemning, Ellicott makes the pair a summing up and a verdict, and Calvin reads the first as condemning outright
Whether inexcusable means inexcusable for judging or without excuse for their own sins: Barnes rules out the first expressly and makes it a statement of their need of another plan of justification

Why Paul withholds the name Jew at this point: Barnes makes it a deliberate rhetorical strategy so the conclusion cannot be evaded, while Wesley takes it as a refusal to acknowledge the man to be a Jew at all
outliers: Gill's naming of Socrates, Cato and Seneca as the seemingly virtuous Gentiles who reproved others and did the same
Gill's third reading, that magistrates of either nation are designed, who may pass with impunity among men but shall not escape the judgment of God
Calvin's saintlings, the hypocrites of outward sanctity who could not be included in the first catalogue of grosser vices
Calvin's Hebraism, which makes the opening particle anticipate a reason rather than draw an inference
Barnes's account of Paul's argumentative skill in approaching the Jews gradually and in the most tender and kind as well as convincing manner
Henry's charge that the Jews thought the Gentiles not worthy to be set with the dogs of their flock, and were themselves sacrilegious if not idolatrous
Theodoret's argument from the judge's own discernment, that the very perfection of their distinguishing convicts them
Clarke's block, which is an analysis of the chapter's whole course rather than a comment on the verse

2.pericope_label: The judgment according to truth and the despised riches of goodness

schools.summary: Gill fixes the judgment meant as not what is exercised on and towards men in this life but what follows after death, called judgment to come, certain, universal as to persons and things, and named the judgment of God in opposition to the judgment of men, because it will be carried on by God only, who is omniscient and omnipotent, and will be definitive. On the riches of goodness he says the apostle anticipates an objection taken from the prosperity of these persons, who might conclude from it that they were not so wicked as he had represented them and would escape the judgment of God, since otherwise they would have been punished in this life; the objection is removed by observing that it was not their innocence but the riches of divine goodness, longsuffering and forbearance which were the causes of their prosperity. By the riches of God's goodness he means not the riches of his special, spiritual and eternal goodness, of which his own people only are partakers, but the general riches of his temporal and providential goodness, which the men of the world commonly have the greatest share of; and by longsuffering and forbearance not his forbearance of his chosen ones, which issues in their salvation, but his forbearance of sinners in not as yet pouring down his wrath. He adds that such persons shall not always go unobserved and unpunished, since a day of wrath and righteous judgment is hastening on and will take place after they have filled up the measure of their iniquity. Calvin's design throughout is to shake hypocrites out of their self-complacencies: they may not think they gain anything though applauded by the world and though they regard themselves guiltless, for a far different trial awaits them in heaven, and since the impurity charged is inward and cannot be proved by human testimony he summons them to the tribunal of God, to whom darkness itself is not hid. God will punish sin without respect of persons in whomsoever it is found, and will not heed outward appearances nor be satisfied with any outward work except what proceeds from real sincerity of heart, so that the mask of feigned sanctity will not prevent him from visiting secret wickedness with judgment; hypocrites are only then awakened when told that God will take account not merely of their disguised righteousness but of their secret motives and feelings. According to truth he calls a Hebrew idiom for inward integrity, opposed not only to gross falsehood but to the outward appearance of good works, and takes it with Grotius of the true state of the case without partiality, the expression being the same in meaning as the righteous judgment of the fifth verse. He raises against himself the rhetorical objection that reproof should not precede proof, and answers that Paul adduced his accusation not before men but appealed to the judgment of conscience, deeming that proved which he had in view, that they could not deny their iniquity if they examined themselves and submitted to the scrutiny of God's tribunal; the sharpness was needed because men of this class trust in themselves with astonishing security unless their vain confidence is forcibly shaken from them, and the best mode of dealing with hypocrisy is to draw it forth to the light of God's judgment. The argument is drawn from the less, since our sins are subject to the judgment of men and much more to that of God, the only true Judge; men are led by a divine instinct to condemn evil deeds, but this is only an obscure and faint resemblance of the divine judgment, and they are extremely besotted who think they can escape the judgment of God though they allow not others to escape their own. On the riches of goodness he denies that there is an argument conclusive on two grounds and takes it as an anticipation of an objection, since hypocrites are commonly transported with prosperity as though they had merited the Lord's kindness and become thus more hardened in their contempt of God; the design of his benevolence is far different, namely to convert sinners to himself, so that where the fear of God does not rule, confidence on account of prosperity is a contempt and a mockery of his great goodness, and a heavier punishment will be inflicted on those whom God has in this life favoured, because in addition to their other wickedness they have rejected his fatherly invitation. When the Lord deals favourably with his servants he makes known his benevolence by symbols and trains them to seek the sum of all good in himself alone; when he treats transgressors with the same indulgence his object is to soften their perverseness by his kindness, and he does not testify that he is already propitious but invites them to repentance, so that if we use not God's bounty for this end we abuse it. Of the verb he says he prefers a rendering more significant than the usual one, taking it not in the sense of driving but of leading as it were by the hand.

Clarke states the principle in a sentence, that God is impartial and will punish sin wheresoever he finds it, and that transgression in a Jew is not less criminal than iniquity in a Gentile. On the fourth verse he asks whether the reader will render of none effect that marked benevolence of God which has given so many superior advantages, and that forbearance which has tolerated his many miscarriages, and that longsuffering which after repeated provocations still continues to bear with him; the word rendered not knowing he takes as not acknowledging, and says the goodness of God manifested in forbearance and longsuffering was designed to accomplish the blessed end of repentance, which want of consideration has hitherto rendered ineffectual. This, he adds, was a maxim among the Jews themselves, for the Synopsis Sohar says that the holy blessed God delays his anger against the wicked to the end that they may repent and be converted. On the fifth verse he traces the sequence, hardness occasioned by a long course of iniquity, an impenitent heart produced by that hardness and callous to the calls and expostulations of conscience, and a treasuring up which is a continual increase of the debt to divine justice. Wesley says we know the judgment of God without thy teaching, that it is God's judgment and not thine, who exceptest thyself from its sentence, that it is just and makes no exception and reaches the heart as well as the life. On the fourth verse he asks whether the man goes farther still, from hoping to escape God's wrath to the abuse of his love, glosses the riches as the abundance and observes that all these are afterwards comprised in the single word goodness, since the man both has sinned, does sin and will sin, and says the goodness is designed of God to lead or encourage him to repentance. On the fifth he turns the irony of the treasury: the man is treasuring up wrath although he thinks he is treasuring up all good things, and what a treasure a man may lay up either way in this short day of life; and it is to himself, not to the man he judges.

Barnes takes we are sure as the common and admitted sentiment of mankind, known and believed generally, implied to be known to the Jews because everywhere taught in the Old Testament and the acknowledged doctrine of the nation, and notes that the apostle so expresses himself as to include them; he cites Calvin by name for the design of the passage, to take away the subterfuges of the hypocrite lest he should pride himself if he obtained the praise of men, since a far more important trial awaited him at the bar of God. According to truth he says is capable of two meanings, the Hebrew use for truly or certainly, and, probably the correct one here, that God will judge not according to appearance but in integrity and righteousness, according to the real nature of conduct and not as it may appear to men, so that the secret sinner and the hypocrite as well as the abandoned profligate must expect to be judged according to their true character. On the third verse he appeals to their deep and instinctive conviction of what was right: if they, imperfect and unholy as they were, condemned such offenders, would not a holy and just God be far more likely to pronounce judgment. The appeal is evidently directed against the Jew, since it was a prevalent sentiment among them that provided they adhered to the rites of their religion God would not judge them with the same severity as the abandoned and idolatrous Gentiles; the apostle shows that crime is crime wherever committed, that sin does not lose its essential character by being committed in the midst of religious privileges, and that those who profess to be the people of God have no peculiar licence to sin, whereas Antinomians in all ages, like the Jews, have supposed that what would be sin in others they may commit with impunity. On despisest he says the word properly means to contemn or treat with neglect, and that they did not professedly treat God's goodness with contempt but perverted and abused it, drawing a practical impression from his forbearance; and on hardness that the word denotes insensibility of mind, that which is insensible to the touch, as a stone. Ellicott says Paul assumes the principle will be acknowledged by Jew and Gentile alike, with a strong under-current of allusion to the way in which the Jew was apt to fall back upon his privileges, since the Jews had an idea that the Gentiles only would be judged while they would claim admission into the Messianic kingdom by right of birth; the principle of judgment will be truth or reality as opposed to appearance, worldly status and formal precedence, asking what a man is and not to what race he belongs, and the emphatic pronoun of the third verse asks whether the Jew is to be the only exception to the rule. On riches he adds a stylometric note, that in this metaphorical sense with reference to the divine attributes the word is peculiar to and characteristic of Paul, used twelve times in his Epistles and not besides in the rest of the New Testament, eight of them in the Epistles of the Imprisonment, three in Romans and one in Second Corinthians, so that the later and earlier Epistles are linked together; and he cautions that arguments of this kind are more important on the positive side than the negative, since the presence of a peculiar usage in two books is an inference of some strength that they are by the same author, while its absence goes a very short way towards the opposite conclusion. He compares the Sinaitic revelation for forbearance and longsuffering, remarks that the moral character thus attributed to God specially distinguished the religion of the Old Testament from that of the surrounding heathen nations, and protests that the fallacy Paul opposes is not yet extinct, since God's goodness is insisted upon as if it were unconditional, whereas the constitution of nature as well as revelation tells us that happiness is annexed to certain acts and a certain frame of mind: the bliss of the Christian is reserved for the Christian and is not showered promiscuously upon all men, otherwise free-will would have no office and righteous dealing no reward. On the fifth verse he says the one condition upon which the goodness of God will come into operation is directly contravened, so that the load of wrath accumulated remains unremoved and only waits for the day of judgment to discharge itself. Robertson glosses judgment as a decision rendered whether good or bad and the preposition as giving the rule of measure, presses the emphatic pronoun as the conceited Jew expecting to escape God's judgment because he is a Jew and finds here a justification of the Baptist's bitter words to the Pharisees and Sadducees, notes that the verb rendered despisest is to think down on, so that this upstart Jew actually thinks down on God, takes the present of leading as conative, kindness trying to lead him to a right-about face and a change of mind and attitude instead of a complacent self-satisfaction and pride of race and privilege, and renders the hardness as an unreconstructed heart with no change in its attitude.

Theodoret says it is evident to those who think rightly that by the divine law all who transgress are obnoxious to punishment, and turns the fourth verse into a direct address: we know indeed that in his own due time the righteous Judge will inflict vengeance on every sinner, but you, who are so ready to punish others and to shut your eyes to your own transgressions, imagine that you will escape the divine tribunal. Not so; God bears with you and has longsuffering because he yet waits your repentance.

debates: What according to truth means: Barnes allows the Hebrew sense of truly or certainly but prefers judgment by the real nature of conduct rather than by appearance, Ellicott makes it reality against status and race, Calvin calls it a Hebrew idiom for inward integrity opposed even to the outward appearance of good works, and Wesley says only that it makes no exception and reaches the heart

Whether Paul reproves before he has proved: Calvin raises the rhetoricians' rule against himself and answers that the accusation was laid not before men but before conscience, and that hypocrisy must be forcibly drawn out into the light of God's judgment

Whether the fourth verse is an argument or an anticipated objection: Calvin denies expressly that it is an argument conclusive on two grounds and Gill agrees that it anticipates an objection drawn from the prosperity of such men, which is answered by distinguishing providential goodness from saving goodness

What the goodness of God is that leads to repentance: Calvin prefers leading as by the hand to driving and Robertson makes the present conative, a kindness that is trying to lead, while Clarke says the end was designed but rendered ineffectual by want of consideration and Ellicott protests that the goodness is not unconditional

Who is meant by the emphatic thou of the third verse: Ellicott asks whether the Jew is to be the only exception to the rule, Robertson makes him the conceited Jew expecting to escape because he is a Jew, and Barnes generalises it into a standing Antinomian error
outliers: Ellicott's stylometric argument from the twelve Pauline uses of riches, eight in the Epistles of the Imprisonment, and his caution that such arguments are stronger positively than negatively
Ellicott's protest that the bliss of the Christian is reserved for the Christian and not showered promiscuously upon all men, otherwise free-will would have no office and righteous dealing no reward
Barnes citing Calvin by name, a rare direct appeal from one voice in the catena to another
Barnes's charge that Antinomians in all ages, like the Jews, have supposed that what would be sin in others they may commit with impunity
Clarke's citation of the Synopsis Sohar, that the holy blessed God delays his anger against the wicked so that they may repent
Robertson's rendering of the verb as to think down on, so that the upstart Jew actually thinks down on God
Gill's distinction between the general riches of providential goodness, which the men of the world have the greatest share of, and the special goodness of God's own people
Wesley's irony that the man thinks he is treasuring up all good things, and treasures to himself and not to the man he judges

6.pericope_label: Judgment according to works, and the two classes it divides

schools.summary: Gill says God will be the Judge, righteous, holy, just and true; every man in particular will be judged, and as the judgment will be general to all so it will be special to every one, proceeding according to their works. Of those who by patient continuance in well doing seek glory he denies the description to the best and most moralised among the Gentiles, since they sought after worldly things, human wisdom and popular applause and not after God, his honour and glory, nor after the immortality which is only brought to light by the Gospel; he denies it also to the pharisaical Jews, who sought righteousness by the works of the law and honour and glory from men and not from God, and to any unregenerate person, and confines it to such as have the true principles of grace implanted in them, whether Jews or Gentiles. The contentious he describes as those who are of the contention, who contend for victory and not truth, strive about words to no profit, and are quarrelsome and sow discord among men and in churches; and the tribulation and anguish he takes as expressive of the second death, the torments of hell, the worm that never dies and the fire that is not quenched. Calvin says the apostle had to do with blind saintlings who thought the wickedness of their hearts well covered provided it was spread over with some disguises of empty works, and therefore pointed out the true character of the righteousness of works which is of account before God, lest they should feel confident that it was enough to pacify him if they brought words and trifles or leaves only. There is not so much difficulty in the verse, he says, as is commonly thought: the Lord will visit the wickedness of the reprobate with just vengeance and recompense them with what they have deserved, and as he sanctifies those whom he has previously resolved to glorify he will also crown their good works, but not on account of any merit; though the verse declares what reward good works are to have, it by no means shows what they are worth or what price is due to them, and it is an absurd inference to deduce merit from reward. On the description of the godly he observes that the word expresses something more than perseverance, for perseverance is not being wearied in constantly doing good, but patience also is required in the saints, by which they may continue firm though oppressed with various trials, since Satan suffers them not to come by a free course to their end. He finds the passage irregular, its tenor interrupted, so that the second clause of the contrast is not cleanly connected with the first, and holds that the meaning is by no means obscure and that we must be satisfied with this in the apostolic writings, eloquence being learnt from other writings while here spiritual wisdom is to be sought, conveyed in a plain and simple style. On the order of Jew and Greek he has no doubt that the Jew is simply placed in opposition to the Gentile, those called Greeks being presently called Gentiles, but that the Jews take precedence because they had, in preference to others, both the promises and the threatenings of the law.

Clarke says that in the day of judgment God will reward and punish every man according as his life and conversation have been, giving eternal life to those who in all the trials and difficulties of the present state have persevered in well doing, seeking for and expecting glory, honour and immortality, and manifesting his indignation and inflicting punishment on all who are contentious, who obstinately dispute against the truth, and who obey unrighteousness, acting under the influence of the principle of sin and not under the influence of the Spirit of God. Misery of all descriptions, without the possibility of escape, will this righteous Judge inflict upon every impenitent sinner, the Jew first as possessing greater privileges and having abused greater mercies, and also the Gentile, who though he had not the same advantages had what God saw fit to give him. Wesley's block on the sixth verse is only the reference to Proverbs; on the seventh he guards the motive, that pure love does not exclude faith, hope and desire; on the eighth he makes the contentious personal, like thee, O Jew, who thus fightest against God, and calls disobedience, stubbornness and impatience the character of a false Jew, hearing in the four words of indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish an allusion to the psalm in which God cast upon the Egyptians the fierceness of his anger. On the ninth he notes that this is the first express mention of the Jews in the chapter, introduced with great propriety, since their having been trained up in the true religion and having had Christ and his apostles first sent to them will place them in the foremost rank of the criminals that obey not the truth.

Barnes takes the sixth verse as a general principle, that God will make retribution as a righteous Judge and give to every man as he deserves, and that in this respect he would deal with the Jew as with the Gentile. Patient continuance he explains as perseverance in well doing, not the performance of one single act but such a course of life as evinces a disposition to obey the law of God, and he leaves the persons undetermined, whoever they may be. The word rendered contentious he says usually denotes a quarrelsome or litigious disposition and generally has reference to controversies among men, but here evidently denotes a disposition towards God, of the same signification as rebellious or as opposing God. Tribulation he explains as the situation of being pressed down by a burden of trials or calamities, and hence by punishment inflicted for sin, denoting as applied to future punishment the pressure of the calamities that will come upon the soul. Ellicott lays down that the apostle here states with unmistakable definiteness and precision the doctrine that works, what a man has done, the moral tenor of his life, will be the standard by which he will be judged at the last day, and that this is the consistent doctrine of Scripture; he then asks how it is to be reconciled with the main theme of the Epistle, the doctrine of justification by faith. His answer distinguishes two sides of Pauline theology, that which is common to all the Jewish schools and developed in direct line from the Old Testament, to which final recompense in accordance with moral action belongs, and that which is peculiar to Paul or developed from scattered germs and from the teaching of our Lord, to which justification by faith belongs, so that a difference of terminology need imply no divergence of idea. The two great classes into which mankind will be divided at the judgment are determined by works, by the tangible outcome of their lives, no opposition between inward and outward being present to the writer's mind, the rule being simply that by their fruits ye shall know them; but if the individual is isolated and considered in his own relations to the Judge, he can neither claim nor expect any reward, since he has broken more commandments than he has kept and the reward promised far exceeds the extent of his obedience, so that his admission must be due to a divine act conditioned by faith, the grace of God making up what he is behind. In the doctrine of final retribution there is thus no opposition between faith and works, and in the doctrine of justification none between works and faith; in the former works may be regarded as the evidence of faith, in the latter as its natural and necessary outcome. On the seventh verse he supplies the verb from the sixth, treats glory and honour and immortality as practically equivalent to eternal life, and puts the stress upon the patient continuance. On the eighth he observes that the construction changes in the Greek, the accusative of the previous verse giving way to a nominative, and that the Authorised rendering contentious is an error through a wrong derivation, the word meaning strictly those who act in the spirit of a hireling and thence, in its secondary sense, those who act in a spirit of factiousness and self-seeking; the mistaken derivation may well have been current in Paul's time, and though Paul distinguishes this word from the proper word for contention that would rather seem to imply some association of ideas, so that factiousness perhaps best expresses the shade of meaning. The two words for anger he distinguishes as the settled angry feeling and the passionate outbreak, and truth here he takes in a moral sense, almost equivalent to rectitude. On the ninth he notes that upon every soul of man is not quite the same as upon every man but more special in character, indicating the part in which the punishment will be felt. Robertson observes that the sixth verse quotes Proverbs and that the rendering will be in accord with the facts, translates the eighth of those who are factious, notes the change of construction there, takes soul of the individual, and remarks that the Jew is first not only in penalty here but in privilege also.

Theodoret turns the sixth verse against the man addressed: since you have an obdurate spirit and remain still in your iniquity, you are passing against yourself the sentence of punishment, which God in mercy yet delays but will in the last day set forth, allotting to each a recompense corresponding to his deeds. On the seventh he says the apostle teaches the difficulties of virtue and displays its crown, the patient continuance in well doing being expressive of those difficulties, in that we must persevere in and carry through our course.

debates: How judgment according to works is to be reconciled with justification by faith: Ellicott raises the question directly and answers it by distinguishing two elements in Pauline theology and two points of view, the classification of mankind by its fruits and the individual's standing before his Judge, while Calvin answers it only by denying that reward proves merit

Whom the patient continuance in well doing describes: Gill excludes the moralised Gentiles, the pharisaical Jews and every unregenerate person and confines it to those with grace implanted, while Barnes leaves the persons undetermined and rests everything on perseverance rather than a single act

What the word rendered contentious means: Ellicott calls the Authorised rendering an error from a wrong derivation and prefers factiousness from the hireling's spirit, Robertson translates factious, Barnes keeps the English word but redirects it from quarrels among men to rebellion against God, and Gill and Clarke keep the sense of contention outright
What patient continuance adds to perseverance: Calvin argues that the word requires patience under trial as well as constancy in doing good, since Satan allows the saints no free course

Why the Jew is named first: Calvin from the promises and threatenings given him in preference to others, Clarke from privileges abused, Wesley from his training in the true religion and the mission of Christ and the apostles to him first, and Robertson noting that the priority holds in privilege as well as in penalty
outliers: Ellicott's rule that no opposition between inward and outward is present to the writer's mind at the judgment, the standard being simply by their fruits ye shall know them
Calvin's maxim that it is an absurd inference to deduce merit from reward
Ellicott's concession that the mistaken derivation behind contentious may itself have been current in Paul's time
Calvin's admission that the passage is irregular and his refusal to look for eloquence in the apostolic writings, where plain and simple style conveys spiritual wisdom
Wesley's hearing of the four words of wrath as an allusion to the psalm on the plagues of Egypt
Ellicott's fine distinction that every soul of man indicates the part in which the punishment will be felt
Gill's charge that the contentious sow discord in churches, which reads the verse against a party spirit among believers

10.pericope_label: No respect of persons, and judgment by the law each man has

schools.summary: Gill takes glory, honour and peace as so many words for the everlasting happiness of the saints, a crown of glory that fadeth not away and an honour exceeding that of the greatest potentates upon earth, since those who enjoy it will be kings and priests and sit with Christ on his throne. On the impartiality of God he lists what will not come into consideration at the day of judgment: of what nation men are, from what parents they are descended, of what age and sex they be, in what state and condition they have lived in this world, nor to what sect they belonged. On the twelfth verse he says this is an instance of the strict justice of God and proves him no respecter of persons, since the Gentiles were without law, that is, without the written law of Moses, though not without the law of nature in their breasts nor without some civil laws and statutes of their own. On the thirteenth he says the apostle shows that the Jews were justly condemned notwithstanding their having and hearing of the law, since hearing without doing it will never denominate persons righteous in the sight of God, however it might recommend them in the sight of men. Calvin says that having hitherto arraigned all mortals generally as guilty, the apostle now brings his accusation home to Jews and Gentiles separately, teaching that the difference between them is no objection, since both without distinction are exposed to eternal death: the Gentiles pretended ignorance as their defence and the Jews gloried in the honour of having the law, and he takes away the subterfuge of the former and deprives the latter of their false and empty boasting, so that the division of the human race into two classes is no reason why both should not be involved in the same guilt. The word rendered person, he explains, is taken in Scripture for all outward things which are wont to be regarded as possessing any value or esteem, so that when we read that God is no respecter of persons we are to understand that what he regards is purity of heart or inward integrity, and that he has no respect for kindred, country, dignity, wealth and similar things, respect of persons here standing for the distinction or difference between one nation and another. On the adverb of the twelfth verse he notes that it commonly bears another sense but that the context requires this one, citing a single Pauline parallel, and that in the former part of the section the apostle assails the Gentiles, to whom no Moses was given to publish and ratify a law from the Lord. On the thirteenth he says the verse anticipates an objection the Jews might have adduced, since having heard that the law was the rule of righteousness they gloried in the mere knowledge of it; to obviate the mistake he declares that the hearing of the law or any knowledge of it is of no such consequence that any one should on that account lay claim to righteousness, but that works must be produced, according to the saying that he who will do these shall live in them. If righteousness be sought from the law the law must be fulfilled, for the righteousness of the law consists in the perfection of works; and they who pervert this passage for the purpose of building up justification by works deserve most fully to be laughed at even by children, so that it is improper and beyond what is needful to introduce a long discussion exposing so futile a sophistry, the apostle urging on the Jews only the decision of the law, that by it they could not be justified unless they fulfilled it, and that if they transgressed a curse was instantly pronounced upon them.

Clarke says that while the finally impenitent Jew and Gentile shall experience the fullest effects of the righteous indignation of the supreme Judge, every man that worketh good, that is, who lives in a conscientious obedience to the known will of God, whether he be Jew or Gentile, shall have glory, honour and peace. The righteous Judge will not act according to any principle of partiality, the character and conduct alone of the persons weighing with him: he will take no wicked man to glory, let his nation or advantages be what they may, and he will send no righteous man to perdition. On the twelfth verse he holds that the Gentiles, who shall be found to have transgressed against the mere light of nature, or rather that true light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world, shall not come under the same rule with the Jews, who have had a written revelation. On the thirteenth he says it does not follow that because one people are favoured with a divine revelation they shall therefore be saved while others who have not had it shall finally perish, since this is not God's procedure where he has given a law. Wesley sets the three terms of the reward against the three of the sentence, glory opposed to wrath and coming from the divine approbation, honour opposed to indignation and coming by divine appointment, and peace now and for ever opposed to tribulation and anguish. On the impartiality of God he adds a caution of his own, that God will reward every one according to his works, but that this is well consistent with his distributing advantages and opportunities of improvement according to his own good pleasure. On the twelfth verse he notes that the apostle speaks of the time past, for all time will be past at the day of judgment, and takes to perish without the law as without regard had to any outward law, the man being condemned by the law written in his heart. On the thirteenth he distinguishes the times of the two clauses, that the hearers of the law are not even now just before God while the doers shall be finally acquitted and rewarded, a most sure and important truth which respects the Gentiles also though principally the Jews.

Barnes explains respect of persons as partiality in pronouncing judgment, and says the particle of the eleventh verse confirms what precedes, particularly that the punishment should be experienced by the Jew as well as the Gentile, since God would deal with both on the principles of justice. On the twelfth verse he insists on the sweep of the declaration, which is not applicable to a few only or to great and incorrigible instances of pagan wickedness but is universal and obviously includes all; to have sinned is to have been guilty of crimes of any kind toward God or man, sin being the transgression of a rule of conduct however made known to mankind, and without law means without revealed or written law, since the apostle immediately says that they had a law of nature. The verb rendered shall perish he traces through its New Testament uses and takes here of future punishment, the destruction of soul and body, opposed to eternal life and therefore denoting eternal death; and he remarks pointedly that the apostle does not say they shall be saved without law, nor give any intimation respecting their salvation, the strain of the argument and this express declaration showing that they who had sinned would be punished, so that if any of the heathen are saved it will be an exception to the general rule, since the apostles evidently believed that the great mass of them would be destroyed and on that ground evinced such zeal to save them. On the thirteenth he says the same sentiment is implied in James and in the Gospels, and that the apostle doubtless designed to meet an objection of the Jews, that they had the law, manifested great deference for it, and heard it read with attention. Ellicott defines respect of persons as regard for the external circumstances of a man as opposed to his internal condition, and here especially regard for the circumstances of birth and race; he finds it interesting that the phrase appears in such different quarters of the New Testament, and observes that the great result of the Christian revelation was to break down the belief in race-religions, the middle wall of partition as Paul calls it, the essential equality of Jew and Gentile before God being unaffected by the precedence of the former in point of time or order, whether as regards punishment or reward. On the twelfth he states the principle that Jew and Gentile alike will be judged, each by the method proper to his case, the Jew by the written law against which he has sinned and the Gentile by the unwritten law of conscience against which he too has sinned, so that the mere hearing of the law will bring no exemption to the Jew. On the thirteenth he argues that the parenthesis should not be placed at this verse, as the Authorised version usually has it, but at the beginning of the next, the present verse being explanatory of what precedes. Robertson notes that Milligan considers the word for respect of persons and its two cognates the earliest definitely known Christian words, found neither in the Septuagint nor in non-Christian writings; he takes the aorist of the twelfth verse as constative and timeless, and the adverb as an old word ordinarily meaning contrary to law or unjustly but here in ignorance of the Mosaic law or of any law, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament. On the thirteenth he observes that the law was read in the synagogue but there was no actual virtue in listening, the virtue being in doing, and compares the like contrast drawn by James between hearers and doers.

Theodoret says that God, being the Maker of all, is therefore the Judge of all, and that he will take account of the Jews and condemn them according to the Mosaic code while dealing otherwise with those who never received it; and on the thirteenth verse he puts the principle in a line, that the law was not sent to us to gratify our ears but to lead us to the practice of what is right.

debates: What respect of persons excludes: Gill lists nation, parentage, age, sex, condition and sect, Calvin extends it to all outward things of value and makes it here the difference between one nation and another, Ellicott narrows it to birth and race and reads the verse as the end of race-religions, and Wesley enters the caution that impartial reward is consistent with unequal distribution of advantages

Whether any of the heathen may be saved: Barnes insists the apostle gives no intimation of their salvation and that the apostles believed the great mass would be destroyed, while Clarke appeals to the true light that lighteth every man and denies that the Gentiles come under the same rule as the Jews

What the adverb rendered without law means: Barnes takes it of the absence of written revelation, Robertson of ignorance of the Mosaic law against its ordinary sense of contrary to law, Calvin notes that the context overrides the common meaning, and Wesley makes it the absence of any outward standard at the judgment

Whether the thirteenth verse supports justification by works: Calvin says those who so pervert it deserve to be laughed at even by children, since the verse only presses the law's own terms, that righteousness by law requires the law fulfilled
Where the parenthesis belongs: Ellicott alone raises it, arguing against the Authorised punctuation that it should begin at the following verse, this one being explanatory of what precedes
outliers: Robertson's report from Milligan that the word for respect of persons and its cognates are the earliest definitely known Christian words, absent from the Septuagint and from non-Christian writers
Ellicott's claim that the great result of the Christian revelation was to break down the belief in race-religions
Wesley's caution that God's impartiality in reward is consistent with his distributing opportunities of improvement according to his own good pleasure
Barnes's inference from the apostles' missionary zeal that they believed the great mass of the heathen would be destroyed
Calvin's refusal to argue at length against justification by works here, on the ground that the sophistry is too futile to need it
Gill's note that the Gentiles were not without civil laws and statutes of their own besides the law of nature
Wesley's observation that the apostle speaks of sinning in the past tense because all time will be past at the day of judgment

14.pericope_label: The Gentiles a law to themselves, and the day when God judges the secrets of men

schools.summary: Gill says the objection of the Gentiles against their condemnation, taken from their being without the law, is here obviated: the apostle owns that they had not the written law of Moses, yet intimates that they had and must have a law against which they sinned and so deserved punishment. Though they had not the law in form, written on tables or in a book, they had the work, the matter, the sum and substance of it in their minds, as appears by the practices of many of them in their external conversation. On the last verse he says the words are to be read in connection with the twelfth and express the time when both Jews and Gentiles will be judged, called a day both because of the clearness and evidence of the judgment that will be made and because a certain time is fixed, though not known, which will surely come. Calvin says the apostle now states what proves the former clause, not thinking it enough to condemn us by mere assertion but proceeding to prove it by reasons, in order to excite us to a greater desire for Christ and a greater love towards him, and showing that ignorance is in vain pretended. By the work of the law is to be understood what the law requires, as the work of God is the work which God requires; and what the Gentiles show is that there is imprinted on their hearts a discrimination and judgment by which they distinguish between what is just and unjust, what is honest and dishonest. He denies that it was so engraven on their will that they sought and diligently pursued it, and holds only that they were so mastered by the power of truth that they could not disapprove of it: why else did they institute religious rites, except that they were convinced that God ought to be worshipped, and why were they ashamed of adultery and theft, except that they deemed them evils? Without reason, therefore, is the power of the will deduced from this passage, as though Paul had said that the keeping of the law is within our power, for he speaks not of the power to fulfil the law but of the knowledge of it; nor is the word heart to be taken for the seat of the affections but only for the understanding, as it is used where the Lord has not given a heart to understand and where men are called slow of heart to believe. His block on the sixteenth verse carries an editorial note that in accordance with some of the fathers, Jerome, Chrysostom, Theophylact and others, Calvin connects the verse with the one immediately preceding, whereas almost all modern critics connect it with the twelfth and consider what intervenes as parenthetic.

Clarke says it does not follow that the Gentiles who have not had a divine revelation shall either perish because they had it not, or that their unrighteous conduct passes unpunished because not having revelation might be considered an excuse. On the phrase by nature he enters a caution at length: much stress has been laid on the word, as if the apostle designed to intimate that nature, independently of the influence of divine grace, possessed such principles as were sufficient to guide a man to glory, but certainly the term cannot be so understood here; he prefers the sense given in Suicer's Thesaurus, truly or in effect, comparing the passage in which those who are served as gods certainly are no gods, that is, are false gods, and citing Cyril of Alexandria's use of the cognate adjective for the union of the two natures in Christ, where natural means true or real. In acting according to justice, mercy, temperance and truth, he says, the Gentiles show that the great object of the law, which was to bring men from injustice, cruelty, intemperance and falsity, is so far accomplished in them, their conscience also bearing witness, that faculty of the soul where the divine light dwells. On the sixteenth verse he takes the gospel clause of what he is now laying down concerning the impartiality of God and his righteous procedure in judging men, not according to their opinions or prejudices, nor according to revelations they never possessed, but according to the various advantages or disadvantages of their political, religious or domestic situation in life. Wesley says the apostle, having refuted the perverse judgment of the Jews concerning the heathens, now speaks directly of the heathens in order to convince the heathens, and that the concession he makes to these serves more strongly to convince the Jews. The work of the law he takes as the substance though not the letter of it, written on their hearts by the same hand which wrote the commandments on the tables of stone, and shown to themselves, to other men and in a sense to God himself; of conscience he says there is none of all its faculties which the soul has less in its power than this. On the sixteenth verse he keeps the connection with the fifteenth, glossing it as who show this in the day, and says that everything will then be shown to be what it really is, the law written in their hearts appearing in that day as it often does in the present life, and that on secret circumstances depends the real quality of actions, frequently unknown to men.

Barnes says the apostle had stated in the previous verse the general principle that only the doers of the law can be justified if justification is attempted by the law, and now proceeds to show that the same principle applies to the heathen, who though they have not the written law of God have sufficient knowledge to be judged. The work of the law he explains as the design or object contemplated by the revealed law, namely to make known to man his duty and to enforce the obligation to perform it, denying that they had all the knowledge which the law would impart. On the sixteenth verse he says it is doubtless to be connected with the twelfth, the intermediate verses being a parenthesis, and that it implies that the heathen world as well as the Jews will be arraigned at the bar of judgment, God judging all in righteousness, the Jew by the law he had and the heathen by the law he had. Ellicott says a sort of parenthesis begins at the fourteenth verse, since the sixteenth refers back to the main subject of the paragraph and not to the particular point on which the apostle digresses, the virtual operation of law among Gentiles as well as Jews. By nature he renders spontaneously, of their own motion, not acting under the coercion of any external rule; the relative he renders inasmuch as they, and the work of the law as the practical effect or realisation of the law, written in their hearts as the original law was written upon the tables of stone. He finds a double witness, since their actions speak for them and conscience witnesses with them. On the sixteenth verse he insists that it takes up the main thread and cannot refer to what immediately precedes, as some would make it, because there the apostle refers to the daily process that goes on whenever doubtful actions are submitted to the law of conscience, whereas here he speaks expressly of the final judgment held by God and not by man; as the Son of God is the Mediator of salvation, so also is he the Mediator of judgment, the function of judgment being specially committed to him, which he calls the consistent teaching of Scripture. On the closing phrase he asks whether the gospel testifies to the simple fact that God will judge the secrets of men or to the particular law or standard by which he will judge them, and thinks the former on the whole preferable. Robertson renders the clause better as that have not the law, that is, the Mosaic law, takes by nature as an instrumental case of an old word from the verb to beget, and says the Gentiles are without the Mosaic law but not without some knowledge of God in conscience, so that when they do right they are a law to themselves; when their conduct corresponds on any point with the Mosaic law they practise the unwritten law in their hearts. The closing phrase he glosses simply as what Paul preaches, and which is the true gospel.

Cyril of Jerusalem turns the verse into a warning: let us dread lest God condemn us, who needs not examination or proofs to condemn. Say not, in the night I committed fornication or wrought sorcery and there was no man by; out of thine own conscience shalt thou be judged, thy thoughts the meanwhile accusing or else excusing. The terrible countenance of the Judge will force thee to speak the truth, or rather, even though thou speak not, it will convict thee, for thou shalt rise clothed with thine own sins or else with thy righteous deeds. And this the Judge himself has declared, for it is Christ who judges, since the Father judges no man but has given all judgment to the Son, not divesting himself of his power but judging through the Son, the wills of the Father and of the Son being not different but one and the same. Theodoret says the apostle shows that the law of nature was written in their hearts, and that the self-condemnation or self-vindication of conscience was according to truth.

debates: What by nature means: Clarke argues at length that it cannot mean nature independent of divine grace and prefers Suicer's sense of truly or in effect, while Ellicott takes it as spontaneously and of their own motion and Robertson merely parses the case

Whether the passage proves a power in the will to keep the law: Calvin denies it expressly, holding that Paul speaks not of the power to fulfil the law but of the knowledge of it, and that heart here means the understanding and not the seat of the affections

What the sixteenth verse connects with: Calvin's block records that Jerome, Chrysostom and Theophylact joined it to the verse immediately before while almost all modern critics join it to the twelfth, Barnes and Ellicott take the modern side, and Wesley alone keeps the older connection

Why the verse cannot refer to what immediately precedes: Ellicott argues that the preceding verses describe the daily process of conscience upon doubtful actions whereas this verse speaks expressly of the final judgment held by God and not by man

What according to my gospel testifies to: Ellicott weighs the fact of judgment against the standard of judgment and prefers the fact, Robertson glosses it as simply what Paul preaches, and Clarke refers it to the impartiality he has been expounding
outliers: Clarke's appeal to Suicer's Thesaurus and to Cyril of Alexandria on the union of the two natures in Christ, to fix the sense of a single adverb
Calvin's argument from pagan practice, that they instituted religious rites because convinced God ought to be worshipped and were ashamed of adultery and theft because they deemed them evils
Ellicott's double witness, the actions speaking for the man and conscience witnessing with them
Wesley's remark that there is none of all its faculties which the soul has less in its power than conscience
Cyril of Jerusalem's warning that a man shall rise clothed with his own sins or with his righteous deeds, and that the Judge's countenance will convict him though he speak not
Wesley's note that on secret circumstances depends the real quality of actions, frequently unknown to men
Ellicott's rule that as the Son is the Mediator of salvation so also is he the Mediator of judgment

17.pericope_label: The Jew’s name and privileges, granted before they are turned against him

schools.summary: Gill says that from this point to the end of the chapter the Jews are particularly addressed, their several privileges and characters being commemorated and allowed them by an ironical concession, several charges being brought against them, even against their principal men, and the plea from circumcision considered, the apostle's whole view being to show what he has been arguing. Knowing his will he takes not of the secret will or purpose of God, nor of his revealed will in the Gospel, of which they were ignorant, but of his declared will in the law, showing what is to be done and what is not. Of their confidence he says they were vainly puffed up in their fleshly minds and strongly persuaded that they were fit persons to be guides; and of the foolish he says that all men in a state of unregeneracy are foolish and need instruction, but that here the common people among the Jews, who knew not the law, are meant, since it was very usual to call any of their doctors and masters an instructor. Calvin weighs the disputed opening: some old copies read the conditional particle, and were it generally received it would meet his approbation, but as the greater part of the manuscripts is opposed and the sense is not unsuitable he retains the old reading, especially as it is only a small difference of one letter, the difficulty with the other being to find a corresponding clause; his block adds that Griesbach has since found a majority of manuscripts in favour of that reading and adopted it. He concedes to the Jews the knowledge of the divine will and the approval of things useful, attained from the doctrine of the law, but distinguishes a twofold approval, one of choice, when we embrace the good we approve, and another of judgment only. More is still granted to them, he says, as though they had not only what was sufficient for themselves but that by which they could enrich others, since he grants that they had such abundance of learning that others might have been supplied from it. The clause about the form of knowledge he takes as a reason for what precedes, because they professed to be the teachers of others, seeming to carry in their breasts all the secrets of the law.

Henry says that in the latter part of the chapter the apostle directs his discourse more closely to the Jews and shows what sins they were guilty of, notwithstanding their profession and vain pretensions. Having said that not the hearers but the doers of the law are justified, he here applies that great truth to the Jews, first allowing their profession and specifying their particular pretensions before turning upon them.

Clarke says that what the apostle had said in the preceding verses being sufficient to enforce conviction on the conscience of the Jew, he now throws off the cover and openly argues with him in the most plain and nervous manner, asserting that his superior knowledge, privileges and profession served only to aggravate his condemnation. To know God's will is to have been favoured with a revelation of it immediately from himself, and the things that are more excellent he renders the things that differ, since the revelation God has given of himself makes the nicest distinctions. In consequence of all these religious advantages, he says, the Jews believed themselves able to teach others and to be guides and lights to the bewildered, darkened Gentiles who might become proselytes to their religion; they believed the Gentiles to be babes and fools compared with themselves, that they alone possessed the only true knowledge, and that they were the only favourites of heaven. Wesley reads the opening as a conditional, and analyses the passage as twice five articles, the former five showing what the Jew boasts of in himself and the other five what he glories in with respect to others, the whole being refuted later in the chapter. Blind, in darkness, ignorant and babes, he says, were the titles which the Jews generally gave the Gentiles; and the form of knowledge and truth he takes as the most accurate knowledge of the truth.

Barnes says that having stated the general principles on which God would judge the world and shown how they condemned the Gentiles, the apostle now proceeds to show how they applied to the Jews, calling their attention with behold as to an important subject and stating their privileges with great skill and address. The knowledge of God's will they obtained from the Scriptures, in which they were distinguished from other nations; the word rendered approvest is capable of two interpretations; and their confidence denotes the full assurance of the Jew that he was superior in knowledge to all other people, it being a remarkable fact that though proud, wicked and hypocritical they put the fullest confidence in their religion. Of the foolish he notes that the word is used in Scripture both of those void of understanding and of the wicked, and takes it here in the former sense. Ellicott calls the Authorised behold an interesting case of a corrupt reading which has found its way into the version, since a decisive consensus of the best manuscripts has but if, the corruption being very obvious and easy; adopting that reading, the answering clause of the sentence is to be found in the question teachest thou not thyself, and the connecting therefore at the beginning of that verse is merely resumptive. He renders his will literally as the will, that is, the supreme will, thinks the Authorised approvest the things that are more excellent probably right though the marginal triest the things that differ is also possible, compares the blind leaders of the blind, and says that the form of knowledge and of the truth is as we might say the presentation of knowledge and of truth, form here not being opposed to substance but implying it. Robertson renders bearest the name, a present passive of an old word found only here in the New Testament, thou art surnamed Jew with Lightfoot, and notes that Jew as opposed to Greek denoted nationality while Hebrew accented the idea of language; restest upon the law he calls a late and rare double compound found in the Septuagint and once in the Didache and elsewhere in the New Testament only in Luke. A guide of the blind he parses as a predicate accusative in indirect discourse, and the corrector of the foolish he takes as an old word for instructor in Plato and probably so here, though it means corrector or chastiser in Hebrews, late inscriptions giving it as instructor.

Chrysostom says that after stating that the Gentile wants nothing appertaining to salvation if he be a doer of the law, and after making that wonderful comparison, the apostle goes on to set down the glories of the Jews, owing to which they thought scorn of the Gentiles, and first the very name itself, which was of great majesty, as the name Christian is now, for even then the distinction which the appellation made was great. Theodoret notes that Paul says not merely named but entitled, the title having been from of old a general and honourable one; to rest in the law is not to weary oneself, like a stranger to the law, in searching after what is right and fitting in practice, but to have the law itself teaching all things plainly, and to boast of God is to boast of one who has honoured him. He glosses the discerning of differences as between things opposite to each other, righteousness and unrighteousness, justice and injustice, temperance and excess, piety and impiety, and says the titles of instructor and teacher point out their arrogant self-opinion and lay bare the superciliousness they exhibited towards proselytes, the divine law having furnished them with the form of knowledge and truth.

debates: Whether the paragraph opens with behold or with but if: Ellicott calls the Authorised reading a corrupt one against a decisive consensus of the best manuscripts, Calvin knew the variant and declined it because most manuscripts then opposed it, his own block recording that Griesbach afterwards found a majority for it, and Wesley prints the conditional

Where the answering clause falls if the conditional is read: Ellicott finds it in the question teachest thou not thyself and makes the therefore there resumptive, while Calvin says the difficulty with that reading is precisely that no corresponding clause can be found

Whether the Jew approves the things that are more excellent or tries the things that differ: Barnes says the word bears both senses, Ellicott prefers the first while allowing the second, Clarke and Theodoret take the second outright, and Calvin cuts across by distinguishing an approval of choice from an approval of judgment

Who the foolish and the babes are: Wesley and Clarke say they are the Gentiles, these being the titles the Jews commonly gave them, while Gill takes them of the common people among the Jews who did not know the law, instructor being the usual title of their own doctors

What form of knowledge means: Ellicott denies that form is opposed to substance here and makes it presentation or embodiment, Wesley takes it as the most accurate knowledge of the truth, and Calvin makes the clause the ground of their claim to teach
outliers: Chrysostom's comparison of the majesty of the name Jew with the name Christian in his own day
Barnes's remark that though proud, wicked and hypocritical the Jews put the fullest confidence in their religion
Gill's reading of the whole list of privileges as an ironical concession
Calvin's editorial sequel, which corrects his own textual judgement by later manuscript evidence
Robertson's note that Jew denoted nationality while Hebrew accented language, and that the verb for resting on the law occurs in the Didache
Theodoret's charge that the titles lay bare the superciliousness the Jews exhibited towards proselytes
Wesley's analysis of the passage as twice five articles, five of self-boasting and five of boasting over others

21.pericope_label: The teacher who does not teach himself, and the name blasphemed through him

schools.summary: Gill says several charges are here brought against the Jews, even against their teachers, and that though they are put by way of question they are to be considered as so many assertions and matters of fact, since though they taught others they did not teach themselves. Adultery he insists is to be taken not figuratively for adulterating the word of God and mixing it with their own inventions, but literally for the sin of adultery, and that not in heart only but in act. Their boast of the law he takes of their having it, which other nations had not, of their knowledge of it, which many of their own people were without or had but a small share of, and of their keeping of it even to perfection. The blasphemy of God's name he extends to the being and perfections of God, such as his holiness, omniscience and omnipotence, which are denied or evil spoken of, and also to the law of God and the forms of worship instituted by him. Calvin notes that this clause and those which follow are commonly put in an interrogatory form, but that some, as Theophylact, Erasmus and Luther, have rendered them as statements, and that there is no difference in the meaning; he thinks it worthy of notice that the apostle follows the Hebrew manner. Sacrilege he fitly compares to idolatry as a thing of the same kind, since sacrilege is simply a profanation of the divine Majesty, a sin not unknown to heathen poets, one of whom calls men sacrilegious for despising the rites of Bacchus. On the dishonouring of God he grants that every transgressor dishonours him, since we are all born to this end, to serve him in righteousness and holiness, yet justly imputes a special fault to the Jews in this respect, since they avowed God as their Lawgiver and yet had no care to form their life according to his rule. The closing quotation he thinks taken from Ezekiel rather than from Isaiah, since in Isaiah there are no reproofs given to the people whereas that chapter in Ezekiel is full of reproofs, though he reports that some take it as a proof from the less to the greater.

Clarke reproduces Dr. Taylor's paraphrase of these verses, that the Jew's pretensions to knowledge and to the office of teaching others signify nothing if he has no regard to his own doctrine, and that he is nothing the better for preaching against theft if he is a thief himself. On the blasphemy of the name he quotes a rabbinic saying that the rulers destroy the influence of their own words among the people, which is done when a rabbin sitting and teaching in the academy says, do not take usury, and himself takes it, or, do not commit rapine, and himself commits it. Wesley says that he does not teach himself who does not practise what he teaches, and traces the order of the charges, that to steal, to commit adultery and to commit sacrilege are to sin grievously against one's neighbour, oneself and God, noting that the apostle had shown the Gentiles first their sins against God, then against themselves, then against their neighbour. His block on the closing quotation is the bare reference to Isaiah.

Barnes says that he who is a teacher of others may be expected to be learned himself, and that by this question the apostle impliedly reproves them for their ignorance, the form of a question being chosen because it conveys the truth with greater force. On adultery he says there is no doubt that this was a crime very common among the Jews, and reports from Grotius that the Jewish Talmud accuses some of the most celebrated of their rabbies by name of this vice, Josephus giving the same account of the nation. To boast in the law, he says, implied their conviction of its excellence and obligation, since a man does not boast of what he esteems to be of no value, so that by boasting they proclaimed their conviction that it was from God while by breaking it they denied it; and their conduct was such as to lead the heathen world to blaspheme and reproach both their religion and its Author, the pagan world being led by their hypocrisy and crimes to despise a religion observed to have no better effect upon its professors. Ellicott refers the connecting particle back to the opening of the paragraph, and on sacrilege says the word properly means to rob temples, that is, idol temples, with a pointed antithesis to that abhorrence of idols on which the Jew prided himself; this is certainly the last offence of which we should have expected the Jews of that date to be guilty, knowing the scrupulousness with which they shunned such things. On the boast of the law he notes that the verse has been regarded not as a question but as a summary answer to the previous questions, that you who make all this boast in the law by breaking it dishonour God, and allows a certain force in the view while observing that the structure of the clause is so similar to those around it. The closing citation he refers to the Septuagint of Isaiah, the sense of the original being that the name of God is dishonoured by the enslavement and oppression of his people, and notes nearer parallels in sense though more remote in words. Robertson describes the break in the syntax, that Paul suddenly abandons the long sentence begun at the opening of the paragraph and starts over with a phrase which gathers it all into small compass and drives it home upon the Jew; the verb rendered abhorrest he calls an old word meaning to make foul or to stink, used in the New Testament only here and in the Apocalypse, and the very word used to express horror of idols. On transgression he calls attention, with Trench, to the mournfully numerous group of words for the varieties of sin, ignorance, violation of law, missing the mark and falling short. The closing words he takes as a free quotation from the Septuagint of Isaiah, and remarks that the Jews were jealous for the Name of God and would not pronounce the Tetragrammaton, and yet acted so that the Gentiles blasphemed that Name.

Theodoret shows that the Jews had drawn no benefit from the establishment of the law among them, being content to pride themselves on its mere letter and endeavouring to teach others while contradicting their teaching by their deeds. On the closing verse he says that not only is such a man not the cause of glory being given to God, but through him many tongues are excited to speak evil of God's name, since when they witness his wicked life they openly reproach the God who has chosen him.

debates: Whether the clauses are questions or assertions: Calvin reports that Theophylact, Erasmus and Luther render them as statements and finds no difference in meaning, Gill treats them as assertions in question form, and Barnes defends the question because it conveys the truth with greater force

Whether the verse on boasting is a question or the summary answer to the questions before it: Ellicott records the second view, allows a certain force in it, and keeps the first on the ground of the clause's structure
