What sacrilege means here: Ellicott and Robertson render it robbing temples and take them to be idol temples, in pointed antithesis to the Jew's abhorrence of idols, while Calvin widens it to any profanation of the divine Majesty and so makes it a thing of the same kind as idolatry

Where the closing quotation comes from: Calvin argues for Ezekiel against Isaiah because Isaiah gives no reproofs to the people, while Ellicott and Robertson both refer it to the Septuagint of Isaiah, Ellicott adding that the sense there concerns the oppression of God's people

Whether adultery is to be read figuratively: Gill rules out the figurative sense of adulterating the word of God and insists on the literal act, while Barnes documents the charge from the Talmud and Josephus
outliers: Ellicott's surprise that Jews of that date should be charged with robbing temples, given the scrupulousness with which they shunned such things
Calvin's appeal to the heathen poets, who called men sacrilegious for despising the rites of Bacchus
Barnes's report from Grotius that the Talmud names celebrated rabbis as guilty of adultery
Clarke's rabbinic parallel of the teacher in the academy who forbids usury and takes it himself
Robertson's irony that the Jews would not pronounce the Tetragrammaton yet acted so that the Gentiles blasphemed the Name
Robertson's citation of Trench on the mournfully numerous group of Greek words for the varieties of sin
Clarke's use of Dr. Taylor's paraphrase in place of comment of his own

25.pericope_label: Circumcision, and who is a Jew inwardly

schools.summary: Gill says the plea from circumcision in favour of the Jews, and of their acceptance with God and justification before him, is here considered, and that the apostle allows circumcision to have been profitable, which must be understood while it was in force. The case of the law-keeping Gentile he takes hypothetically, if any such persons could be found among the Gentiles who keep the whole law of God, and holds that it can be absolutely understood only of such as from a principle of grace act in obedience to the law as it is in the hands of Christ. Uncircumcision by nature he explains by contrast: as circumcision was by the command of God and performed by the art of men, uncircumcision is by nature and what men naturally have. The plea from name and privilege he removes by distinguishing between a Jew and a Jew and between circumcision and circumcision, the true Jew being one who has an internal work of grace upon his soul, who has not only an outward name but an inward nature, not the law of God in the hand but in the heart, not an external righteousness only but internal holiness. Calvin says the apostle dissipates by anticipation what the Jews might have objected in defence of their own cause, since circumcision was a symbol of the Lord's covenant by which he had chosen Abraham and his seed as his peculiar people, so that they seemed not to have gloried in vain. Against them he sets a very strong argument: everything is below its end and subordinate to it, and since circumcision looks to the law it must be inferior to the law, so that it is a greater thing to keep the law than to have the circumcision instituted for its sake, whence it follows that the uncircumcised who keeps the law is the better placed. The phrase by the letter he calls a figure of speech, a substitution by which a noun is put in a form different from its obvious import, meaning the literal circumcision, and he denies that the apostle means they violated the law because they had that circumcision. The real Jew, he concludes, is not to be ascertained either by natural descent, or by profession, or by an external symbol, and the circumcision which constitutes a Jew does not consist in an outward sign only, but both are inward; he calls the outward rite without piety the letter and the spiritual design of the rite the spirit, since the whole importance of signs and rites depends on what is designed, and when the end in view is not regarded the letter alone remains.

Henry says that no forms, ordinances or notions can profit without regenerating grace, which will always lead to seeking an interest in the righteousness of God by faith; for a man is no more a Christian now than he was really a Jew of old who is only one outwardly, neither is that baptism which is outward in the flesh.

Clarke says it is a blessing to belong to the Church of God and to wear the sign of the covenant, provided the terms of the covenant are complied with, but that if a man does not observe the conditions the outward sign is without meaning. Of the Gentile who keeps the law he says that if he is found to act according to the spirit and design of the law, acting uprightly according to the light which God has afforded him, it will be reckoned to him as if he were circumcised and had walked agreeably to the law; and uncircumcision by nature he takes of the Gentile who by the custom of his country and by birth is not obliged to be circumcised. The true Jew he calls a genuine member of the Church of God, as against one who has only an outward profession, and he says that circumcision is a rite which represents a spiritual thing, the change and purification of the heart, so that the true Jew is one whose heart is purified according to what God has uniformly prescribed by his prophets, his circumcision being of the heart, in the spirit, by the Spirit of God. Wesley marks that the apostle does not say circumcision justifies, and that the Jew's circumcision is become uncircumcision already in effect, so that he will have no more benefit by it than if he had never received it. The Gentile who keeps the law he describes as walking agreeably to it, and asks whether his uncircumcision shall not be counted for circumcision in the sight of God; uncircumcision by nature he takes of those who are literally uncircumcised, fulfilling the law as to the substance of it and condemning in that day the man who has the bare literal circumcision. The true Jew is one of God's people, one inwardly in the secret recesses of his soul, the acceptable circumcision being that of the heart, which he refers to the promise in Deuteronomy and describes as the putting away of all inward impurity.

Barnes explains circumcision as the peculiar rite by which the relation to the covenant of Abraham was recognised, or by which the right to all the privileges of a member of the Jewish commonwealth was acknowledged, to which the Jews of course affixed a high importance. Of the Gentile who keeps the righteousness of the law he says it could not be supposed that a heathen would understand the requirements of the ceremonial law, so that the reference must be to the moral law. Uncircumcision which is by nature he takes as the natural state of man, his condition before he is admitted to any of the peculiar rites of the Jewish religion, and to judge thee as to condemn thee as guilty. On the true Jew he says that he who is merely descended from Abraham and is circumcised and externally conforms to the law does not possess the true character or manifest the true spirit contemplated by the separation of the Jewish people, whereas the Jew inwardly comes up to the design of the Jewish institution and manifests truly what it is to be a Jew, being in heart a Jew and fulfilling the design of their being separated as a peculiar people. Ellicott glosses the verb of the twenty-fifth verse as is become, that is, ipso facto reduced to the case of the uncircumcised. On the judging of the twenty-seventh he compares the saying that the men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation and shall condemn it, and says the idea is that of putting to shame by contrast; by the letter he explains as marking the condition or circumstance under which the action is done, so that it might be paraphrased with all the advantages of the written law and of circumcision, and he adds that here again the sentence may not be a question but an affirmation. Robertson takes the condition of the twenty-fifth verse as a third-class condition with a verb meaning to do as a habit, and says the Jew is then like the Gentile, with no privilege at all; the condition of the twenty-sixth he calls a mere supposition, in which Paul means keeping on keeping the law perfectly, and the participle of the twenty-seventh he takes of a fulfilling continued to the end, as would be necessary. He notes the unusual position of the pronoun so far from its verb, and on the last verses supplies the ellipsis, the in the open Jew, with circumcision, phylacteries and tithes, against the in the inward part Jew, whose circumcision of the heart is no mere surgical operation.

Theodoret says the holy apostle follows in the train of the ancient prophecies, since the God of all says by Jeremiah that all the Gentiles are uncircumcised in flesh and all the house of Israel uncircumcised in heart. The law, he says, demands practice: when the circumcised man has not this and the uncircumcised has, the first ought justly to be called a sinner and the second to receive the name. He calls worthy of all admiration the exceeding greatness of the apostle's wisdom in the way he turns the natural condition of the Gentile against the privileged Jew, and on the last verse falls back upon the testimony of the prophetic writings already quoted.

debates: How far circumcision profits: Wesley notes pointedly that the apostle does not say it justifies, Gill limits the profit to the time while the rite was in force, Clarke makes it conditional on complying with the covenant, and Calvin treats the whole as an objection dissipated by anticipation

Whether the law-keeping Gentile is a real case or a supposition: Gill says the words are spoken hypothetically and Robertson calls it a condition of mere supposition requiring perfect and continued obedience, while Clarke takes the case as real and says such a man's uprightness will be reckoned to him as circumcision
Which law the Gentile is imagined to keep: Barnes rules out the ceremonial law, which no heathen could be supposed to understand, and confines the reference to the moral law
Why keeping the law outweighs the rite: Calvin argues from subordination, that circumcision looks to the law and is therefore inferior to it, everything being below its end
Whether the twenty-seventh verse is a question or an affirmation: Ellicott raises the possibility of an affirmation here as he did earlier in the chapter, while the others read it as a question
outliers: Wesley's four-word limit, that the apostle does not say circumcision justifies
Calvin's principle that everything is below its end and subordinate to it, applied to a rite against the law it serves
Calvin's definition of letter and spirit as the outward rite without piety and the spiritual design of the rite
Ellicott's rendering of judge thee as putting to shame by contrast, on the model of the men of Nineveh
Robertson's gloss on the open Jew as the Jew of circumcision, phylacteries and tithes, against the inward Jew whose circumcision is no surgical operation
Theodoret's admiration for the apostle's wisdom in turning the Gentile's natural condition against the privileged Jew
Henry's extension of the argument to baptism, that a man is no more a Christian now than he was really a Jew of old who is only one outwardly
